episodes.text: Underwent a religious conversion at 14 and served as a junior minister for three years, then gradually and independently came to question and abandon core tenets he had once preached.
Directly, publicly charged in September 1963 that the FBI itself was "a hazard to the Civil Rights Movement," naming Hoover as effectively siding with segregationists.
Lost all four unpublished novel manuscripts he had written before relocating to Paris and did not stop writing.
Had a manuscript rejected by Harper's and simply set it aside to work on another project.
Sustained a demanding personal revision practice across years for individual pieces.
Left the United States for Paris in November 1948 with only $40 and a bag of unfinished manuscripts.
Continued public political writing and activism despite being the subject of the largest FBI file ever compiled on any African American artist of the Civil Rights era (1,884 pages, 1958-1974).
Publicly debated a prominent ideological opponent, William F. Buckley Jr., at Cambridge University (1965) and won decisively.

Developed and sustained a specific, demanding personal revision standard, sometimes spending years refining a single essay, articulated directly in his own words: "rewriting [is] very painful... you know it's finished when you can't do anything more to it."
Won the 1965 Cambridge Union debate against William F. Buckley Jr. on the motion "Is the American Dream at the expense of the American Negro?" by a lopsided, quantified margin (544 votes to 164).
Found genuine refuge in reading at the public library from a young age as an alternative to a difficult home environment.
Began writing across multiple forms (poems, short stories, plays) early.
